theory.title: NAT: One Address for Many
theory.recap: DHCP gave you a private address (192.168.1.5) and you know how to resolve names with DNS. But private addresses are not routable on the public internet. To reach a public destination you must look up its name AND translate your source address. Routing happens before, between, and after.
theory.plainObjective: Resolve fcc.io with DNS, then cross the NAT gateway to swap your private source IP for a public one, then route on to the public destination.
theory.summary: NAT is running right now on your home router. Your laptop, phone, and every device at home share a single public IP - and your router silently translates every packet in and out, invisibly.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Why private IPs exist
bodyParagraphs.text: IPv4 has about 4 billion addresses - not enough for every device on earth. RFC 1918 set aside three ranges (10.x.x.x, 172.16-31.x.x, 192.168.x.x) for private use. Your DHCP server in the last act gave you one of these. They're free to reuse inside any home or office - but public internet routers will not forward them.

bodyParagraphs.heading: What NAT does
bodyParagraphs.text: A NAT gateway sits at the boundary between private and public. When your packet crosses it, the gateway replaces your private source IP with its own public IP. Return traffic comes back to the gateway, which translates it back and forwards it to you.

bodyParagraphs.heading: The trade-off
bodyParagraphs.text: NAT stretches the IPv4 address space dramatically - millions of devices can share one public IP. The cost is complexity: the gateway must track every active connection and the internet cannot directly initiate connections to devices behind NAT.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Order of operations
bodyParagraphs.text: Your destination is a name (fcc.io). Resolve it at DNS first - your packet has no destIP until then. With the IP in hand, R1's table decides where to send you next. The public-bound route leads to the NAT gateway; from there a second router carries you across the public network.

theory.mission:
You are 192.168.1.5 trying to reach fcc.io.

Resolve the name at the DNS resolver, then let R1 route you to the NAT gateway. After NAT rewrites your source IP, R2 will carry you the rest of the way. Watch the top bar as your IP changes.

termIntroductions.headline: Private IP
termIntroductions.body: Addresses starting with 192.168, 10, or 172.16-31 are reserved for private networks (RFC 1918). They are free to reuse inside any home or office, but public internet routers will not forward them. You need NAT to reach the outside.

termIntroductions.headline: NAT - Network Address Translation
termIntroductions.body: The gateway swaps your private source IP for its own public IP before forwarding. From the internet's perspective, all traffic from your network comes from one address - the gateway's. Your original IP is hidden.

termIntroductions.headline: Public IP
termIntroductions.body: A globally unique address routable on the internet. After NAT, your packet appears to come from 203.0.113.1 - the gateway's public IP. The server at 8.8.8.1 never sees 192.168.1.5.
